# Summary & Logic
This document presents the statistical models testing Question 1: Worry-outcome coupling. 
We examine whether morning worry about interference predicts actual evening 
interference on the same day, controlling for pain context and concurrent affective states. 
The analysis uses multiply imputed data (m=28 imputations) with linear mixed-effects models
accounting for repeated daily assessments nested within participants.

All models use Rubin's pooling rules to combine estimates across imputations, thereby 
accounting for missing data uncertainty in parameter estimates, standard errors, and significance tests.

```{r message = F, echo=FALSE}
# importing the MIDS array

imp_1_with_trends<-readRDS("c:/Documents and Settings/d.vitali/Desktop/Github/CRIISP-WP6/Data/imp_1_with_trends_m28_12_05_25.rds") 
```

# Q1: LMM for pred./Exp. coupling

The worry-outcome coupling model tests whether morning predictions about interference 
have predictive validity for actual evening interference. 

## DAG

The directed acyclic graph (DAG) shows our assumed causal structure. Morning worry 
(exposure) and pain context both directly predict evening interference (outcome), 
while mood and stress act as common causes of both worry and interference. Age and 
study day are included as background covariates. The random intercept structure is 
not shown in this DAG but it is included in the model allowing these relationships 
to vary around person-specific baselines.

```{r message = F, echo=FALSE}


# Visualize the causal structure for Q1 using a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
# The DAG represents our theoretical assumptions about how morning worry,
# pain context, and affective states jointly predict evening interference.

dag_Q1 <- dagify(
  Interference ~ Worry + Pain + Mood + Stress + Age_c + Day_count,
  Worry ~ Pain + Mood + Stress + Age_c + Day_count,
  
  exposure = "Worry",
  outcome = "Interference",
  
  labels = c(
    Interference = "Evening\nInterference",
    Worry = "Morning\nWorry (t)",
    Pain = "Pain Trend\n(t-1 to t-3)",
    Mood = "Morning\nMood (t)",
    Stress = "Morning\nStress (t)",
    Age_c = "Age (centred)",
    Day_count = "day count" 
  ),
  
  coords = list(
    x = c(Worry = 1, Interference = 2, Pain = 0, Mood = 1, Stress = 1, Day_count = 0.1,Age_c = 0.1),
    y = c(Worry = 0, Interference = 0, Pain = -1, Mood = -1, Stress = 1, Day_count = 1,Age_c = 0.5)
  )
)


# Plot with ggdag
ggdag_Q1_bw<-ggdag(dag_Q1, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(title = "Q1: Worry-Outcome Coupling Model",
       subtitle = "Morning worry predicting evening interference",
       caption = "Confounders: Pain trend (t-1 to t-3), Morning mood, Morning stress and Age (centred)") +
    theme_dag_blank() 

ggdag_Q1<-ggdag_status(dag_Q1, text = FALSE, use_labels = "label") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("exposure" = "#2C7BB6", "outcome" = "#D7191C", "latent" = "gray70"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Q1: Worry-Outcome Coupling Model",
       subtitle = "Morning worry predicting evening interference",
       caption = "Confounders: Pain trend (t-1 to t-3), Morning mood, Morning stress, Age (centred)") +
  theme_dag_blank() 
ggdag_Q1
```




The baseline model  in the DAG tests morning worry about interference (interf_worry) as a significant predictor of evening interference, with a positive coefficient indicating that higher morning predictions correspond to higher evening interference ratings. 


## Model Specifications and Comparisons

We fit three primary models and several sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the worry-interference coupling estimate.

* Model 0 (Baseline): Tests worry-interference coupling controlling for pain trend and current affective states
* Model 0a (Trend alternative): Same as model 0 but substitutes trend measures for current affective states

two models that extend model 0:

* Model 1 (Pain deviation): Extends model 0 adding acute pain fluctuation as predictor
* Model 2 (Interaction): Extends model 1 testing whether worry-interference coupling varies by acute pain

and an additional sensitivity analysis for the autocorrelation structure of evening interference:
* Model 1_autocorr: Controls for autoregressive structure of evening interference


All models are pooled using Rubin´s Rules. RR are designed to pool parameter estimates, such as mean differences, regression coefficients, standard errors and to derive confidence intervals and p-values.
[https://bookdown.org/mwheymans/bookmi/rubins-rules.html]

This means that by pooling parameter estimates we get the pooled means of the same parameter estimated across all imputed datasets. 

This is helpful to reflect the uncertainty around the imputation we have done in our parameter estimates. Using mice::pool() we get appropriate standard errors estimates that reflect both within-imputation variance (the average of the standard errors from each dataset), and between-imputation variance (the variability in parameter estimates across the imputed datasets). Degrees of freedom are also adjusted to account for the number of imputations and the for the proportion of missing data; P-values, confidence intervals, and test statistics use the pooled estimates and variances so they appropriately reflect the extra uncertainty resulting from missing data imputation. 
[https://bookdown.org/mwheymans/bookmi/rubins-rules.html#significance-testing]

```{r message = F}

# Fit Q1 models testing worry-outcome coupling across 28 imputed datasets.
# Model 0: Baseline with pain trend and current affective states
# Model 0a: Alternative using trend variables for stress/mood instead of current values

model_Coupling_pooled_0 <- with(imp_1_with_trends, 
                    lmer(evening_interference ~ interf_worry + 
                        pain_trend_3d +
                        morning_mood + 
                        morning_stress + 
                        day_count + 
                        Age_c +
                        (1 | alias)))
model_Coupling_pooled_0a <- with(imp_1_with_trends, 
                    lmer(evening_interference ~ interf_worry + 
                        pain_trend_3d +
                        stress_trend_3d + 
                        mood_trend_3d + 
                        day_count + 
                        Age_c +
                        (1 | alias)))
```

We compare Model 0 (current mood/stress) against Model 0a (trend mood/stress) 
using information criteria to determine which specification better captures the 
affective contribution to interference.


```{r message = F}
AIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0 <- mean(sapply(model_Coupling_pooled_0$analyses, AIC))
AIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0a <- mean(sapply(model_Coupling_pooled_0a$analyses, AIC))

BIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0 <- mean(sapply(model_Coupling_pooled_0$analyses, BIC))
BIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0a <- mean(sapply(model_Coupling_pooled_0a$analyses, BIC))


# Compare model fit using information criteria averaged across imputations
# Lower AIC/BIC indicates better balance of fit and parsimony
# Comparing model 0 (current mood/stress) vs 0a (trend mood/stress)
rbind(
  AIC_Coupling_pooled_mean_0 = AIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0,
  AIC_Coupling_pooled_mean_0a = AIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0a,
  BIC_Coupling_pooled_mean_0 = BIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0,
  BIC_Coupling_pooled_mean_0a = BIC_model_Coupling_pooled_0a
) %>% kable
```

Then we test the extended models (model 1 and 2) to examine whether adding acute 
pain fluctuations (deviation from trend) and their interaction with worry improves 
model fit beyond the baseline specification.

The D1 test implements a Wald test for multiply imputed data, combining test 
statistics across imputations using Rubin's rules. Significant p-values (<0.05) 
indicate that the added predictor(s) significantly improve model fit.

```{r message = F}
# pain_deviation_from_trend = morning_pain - pain_trend_3d,
model_Coupling_pooled_1 <- with(imp_1_with_trends, 
                    lmer(evening_interference ~ interf_worry + 
                        pain_deviation_from_trend + 
                        pain_trend_3d +
                        morning_mood + 
                        morning_stress + 
                        day_count + 
                        Age_c +
                        (1 | alias)))

model_Coupling_pooled_2 <- with(imp_1_with_trends, 
                    lmer(evening_interference ~ interf_worry * pain_deviation_from_trend + 
                        pain_trend_3d +
                        morning_mood + 
                        morning_stress + 
                        day_count + 
                        Age_c +
                        (1 | alias)))


# Compare nested models using D1 statistic (Wald test for multiply imputed data)
# D1 tests whether adding pain_deviation_from_trend improves fit beyond model_0
# Null hypothesis: additional predictor has zero effect
D1(model_Coupling_pooled_1, model_Coupling_pooled_0)
D1(model_Coupling_pooled_2,model_Coupling_pooled_1)
```

### Sensitivity Analysis for Lagged Effect Of Interference

We test whether the worry-interference coupling remains robust when controlling 
for autoregressive structure in evening interference (i.e., whether yesterday's 
interference predicts today's interference beyond current predictors).
```{r message = F}
# sensitivity analysis controlling for autocorrelation
model_Coupling_pooled_autocorr <- with(imp_1_with_trends, 
                    lmer(evening_interference ~ interf_worry + 
                        lagged_evening_interference +
                        pain_trend_3d +
                        morning_mood + 
                        morning_stress + 
                        day_count + 
                        Age_c +
                        (1 | alias)))
Q1_Sens_A_pooled_summary <- summary(pool(model_Coupling_pooled_autocorr), conf.int = TRUE) 

Q1_Sens_A_pooled_summary <-Q1_Sens_A_pooled_summary %>%mutate(
  estimate = round(estimate, 3),
  std.error = round(std.error, 3),
  statistic = round(statistic, 3),
  df = round(df, 2),    # degrees of freedom often rounded to 2 decimals
  p.value = round(p.value, 3),
  `2.5 %` = round(`2.5 %`, 3),
  `97.5 %` = round(`97.5 %`, 3)
)

kableExtra::kable(Q1_Sens_A_pooled_summary[1:8])

```

## Multicollinearity (pooled)
We calculate Variance Inflation Factors using [check_collinearity()](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/performance/versions/0.12.4/topics/check_collinearity) from the [performance](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/performance/versions/0.12.4)  quantify how much predictor standard 
errors are inflated due to correlations with other predictors. VIF < 5 indicates 
acceptable collinearity; VIF > 10 suggests serious multicollinearity requiring 
model revision.
```{r message = F}


# Check variance inflation factors (VIF) to detect multicollinearity
# VIF > 5 suggests problematic correlation between predictors
# Only checking first imputed dataset (pattern consistent across imputations)
check_collinearity(model_Coupling_pooled_0$analyses[[1]])
```

```{r message = F}
Q1_pooled_summary <- summary(pool(model_Coupling_pooled_0), conf.int = TRUE) # The pool() function combines the estimates from m repeated complete data analyses

# Round relevant columns to 3 decimal places (adjust as needed)

  estimate = round(estimate, 3),

  p.value = round(p.value, 3),

)

# Print rounded table
# pain_deviation_from_trend = morning_pain - pain_trend_3d,
kableExtra::kable(Q1_pooled_summary[1:8])


```


## Variance explained (pooled)

We decompose the total variance in evening interference into components explained 
by fixed effects (predictors), random effects (between-person differences), 
and residual (unexplained within-person fluctuation).
```{r}

# Decompose variance explained using Nakagawa's R² for mixed models.
# R²_marginal = variance explained by fixed effects (predictors)
# R²_conditional = total variance explained (fixed + random effects)
r2_list <- lapply(model_Coupling_pooled_0$analyses, function(fit) {
  r2 <- r2_nakagawa(fit)
  c(R2_marginal = r2$R2_marginal, 
    R2_conditional = r2$R2_conditional)
})

# Pool across imputations
r2_pooled <- colMeans(do.call(rbind, r2_list))

# Extract values properly (remove names)
r2_marginal <- as.numeric(r2_pooled[1])
r2_conditional <- as.numeric(r2_pooled[2])
r2_random <- r2_conditional - r2_marginal
r2_residual <- 1 - r2_conditional

# Create visualization data
variance_components <- data.frame(
  Component = c("Fixed Effects (Predictors)", 
                "Random Effects (Between-Person)", 
                "Residual (Unexplained)"),
  Variance = c(r2_marginal, r2_random, r2_residual) * 100
)

variance_components %>% kable
```


### Additional Diagnostics
We examine additional model fit diagnostics using one representative imputed dataset (imputation 1). 

```{r message = F}
# Extract first imputed dataset for diagnostic checking
model_data<-complete(imp_1_with_trends, 1)

# Clean data: drop NAs from lagging (matches lmer's internal dropping)
model_data_clean <- model_data %>% 
  filter(!is.na(lagged_evening_interference))

mod_pain_coupling_unc <- lmer(evening_interference ~ 1+ (1 | alias), data = model_data,REML = FALSE)



# model with 3d pain trend
mod_pain_coupling_0_one_sample <-  lmer(
  evening_interference ~ interf_worry + 
                         pain_trend_3d +
                         morning_mood + 
                         morning_stress +
                         day_count +
                         Age_c +
                        (1 | alias),  
  data = model_data_clean,
  REML = FALSE  # Important for model comparison

)

```

check_model() from the performance package provides the visual check of 
various model assumptions: 
* normality of residuals
* normality of random effects
* linear relationship
* homogeneity of variance 
* multicollinearity

```{r message = F, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
check_model(mod_pain_coupling_0_one_sample, check = c("all"))
```

#### Autocorrelation
* ACF plot aid visual examination of autocorrelation (lines should stay within bands)
* Box-Ljung test Model residuals approximate white noise (should not be significant).
```{r}
residuals <- resid(mod_pain_coupling_0_one_sample)
############## AUTOCORRELATION diagnostics #####################
# Check model residuals' autocorrelation structure against white noise
# ACF estimates the autocovariance or autocorrelation function
# ACF is useful for identifying the order of the MA (Moving Average) component
acf(residuals, main = "ACF of Model Residuals (Imputation 1)")
# PACF estimates the partial autocorrelations. Same as acf but pacf controls for 
# for the influence of intermediate lags. this way focuses only on the effect of immediate lags
#pacf(residuals, main = "PACF of Model Residuals")

#
Box.test(residuals, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
## plot residuals vs day_count to see autocorrelation trends within participants
ggplot(model_data_clean, aes(x = day_count, y = residuals, group = alias)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) +
  labs(x = "Day Count", y = "Residuals", title = "Residuals vs Day Count") +
  theme_minimal()
############## END AUTOCORRELATION #####################

# VIF Thresholds
#    VIF < 5: No multicollinearity concern
#    VIF 5-10: Moderate multicollinearity (often acceptable)
#    VIF > 10: Severe multicollinearity (problematic)

# VIFs (~6-7) are within acceptable bounds and much lower than the severe threshold.
# Some collinearity is expected for Interaction Models because interaction terms often 
# correlate with their component terms and deviation scores often correlate with each 
# other when calculated from related time series.
```


## Coefficient Visualization

We visualize the pooled coefficient estimates from Model 0 (baseline) to compare 
the relative magnitude of predictors. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.
```{r message = F, warning=FALSE}


pooled_summary <- summary(pool(model_Coupling_pooled_0), conf.int = TRUE)

# Prepare data from your pooled results
coef_data <- pooled_summary %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Create cleaner labels
    term_label = case_when(
      term == "interf_worry" ~ "Worry about\nInterference",
      term == "pain_trend_3d" ~ "Pain Trend\n(3-day)",
      term == "morning_mood" ~ "Morning\nMood",
      term == "morning_stress" ~ "Morning\nStress",
      term == "day_count" ~ "Study\nDay",
      term == "Age_c" ~ "Age (centred)",
      TRUE ~ term
    ),
    # Flag significance
    significant = ifelse(p.value < 0.05, "sig", "ns"),
    # Reorder by absolute effect size
    term_label = reorder(term_label, abs(estimate))
  )

# Plot
ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = estimate, y = term_label, color = significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = `2.5 %`, xmax = `97.5 %`), 
                 width = 0.2, size = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("sig" = "#2C7BB6", "ns" = "#D3D3D3"),
                     guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient (b) with 95% CI", 
       y = "",
       title = "Worry-Outcome Coupling: Daily Predictors of Interference",
       caption = "Morning worry and contextual factors predicting evening pain interference (pooled estimates, m = 28)")+ 
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 2, face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = -2, size = 9, color = "gray40")
  )
```
